q: What is the never-exceed speed (Vne) of the Seneca I?

d: 190 MPH CAS
207 MPH CAS
195 MPH CAS

q: What is the maximum structural cruising speed (Vno) of the Seneca I?
a: 190 MPH CAS
d: 217 MPH CAS
146 MPH CAS
175 MPH CAS
why: Vno is 190 MPH CAS, the top of the green arc. Above it, in the yellow arc up to 217 MPH, fly only in smooth air.

a: 146 MPH CAS
d: 133 MPH CAS
125 MPH CAS
150 MPH CAS

190 MPH
125 MPH

q: What is the maximum flaps-extended speed (Vfe) of the Seneca I?
a: 125 MPH CAS
d: 150 MPH CAS
105 MPH CAS
140 MPH CAS

150 MPH for both
125 MPH for both

q: You are descending at 140 MPH CAS. Which landing gear operation is within limits?

d: Retracting the gear, but not extending it
Neither extending nor retracting it
Both extending and retracting it

105 MPH CAS, radial blue line
69 MPH CAS, bottom of white arc

80 MPH, single-engine minimum control
125 MPH, maximum flaps extended

a: 76 to 190 MPH
d: 69 to 190 MPH
80 to 217 MPH
76 to 217 MPH

69 to 150 MPH
65 to 125 MPH

Demonstrated crosswind component 17 MPH
Maximum crosswind component 25 MPH

Normal category; spins approved with gear up only
Utility category; no acrobatic maneuvers except spins

190 MPH maximum; Vmc 81 MPH

4.0 to 5.0 in. Hg
3.5 to 4.5 in. Hg

q: What does the instrument panel placard say about single-engine stalls?

Not recommended; can cause 1,000 ft loss and 30° bank
Permitted only above 3,500 ft with props unfeathered

a: Sea level standard conditions
d: Maximum gross weight at 5,000 ft
Any altitude and temperature
The single-engine service ceiling

About 72 MPH CAS
About 58 MPH CAS

About 65 MPH CAS, 15 MPH below Vmc
About 80 MPH CAS, equal to Vmc

95 MPH CAS
87 MPH CAS

IO-360-C1E6 on both sides
TIO-360-C1E6 on the left; LTIO-360 on the right

Any premium automotive gasoline

Green 14–35 PSI; red line at 35 PSI only

20.6 GPH
16.5 GPH

q: When does the AFM say the cowl flaps should be open?
a: During ground operations and in climbs
d: Only during takeoff and go-around
During descents and landing
Only when CHT nears the red line
why: Cowl flaps give manual control of engine temperature. In no case may CHT exceed 475°F or oil temperature 245°F.

q: Above what engine RPM must the propeller be turning for it to feather?
a: 800 RPM
d: 500 RPM
why: Below about 800 RPM, loss of centrifugal force lets a stop pin engage. The pin keeps the prop from feathering every time the engine is shut down on the ground.

q: An engine fails and you delay. Before you move the prop control, the engine slows below 800 RPM. What happens?
a: Stop pins engage and the prop will not feather
d: The prop feathers normally, just more slowly
The prop feathers once the mixture is cut off
The prop feathers when the throttle is closed
why: The props feather only while turning above 800 RPM. If RPM drops below that, the centrifugal stop pins engage and hold the blades out of feather, leaving a draggy unfeathered prop.

q: What does the AFM give as the cause of a propeller overspeed?
a: Loss of the air charge in the prop dome
d: A broken governor control cable
Cold oil during a winter climb
Feathering stop pins that fail to engage
why: Losing the dome air charge can let the prop overspeed if the throttle is advanced rapidly or airspeed is abruptly increased. The AFM adds that an overspeeding prop will not feather, so use the overspeed procedure instead.

q: After recovering from a propeller overspeed, what can cause it to happen again?
a: Throttle below 15–20 in. MP above 105 MPH, then adding power
d: Any RPM above 2400 with the prop control fully forward
Climbing above 10,000 ft at full throttle and 2700 RPM
Throttle below 15–20 in. MP below 105 MPH, then adding power
why: The AFM warns that retarding the throttle below 15–20 inches MP at speeds above 105 MPH may let the prop overspeed again when power is reapplied. Use the same procedure to regain control.

q: What are the Seneca I maximum takeoff and maximum landing weights?

4,200 lb takeoff; 4,200 lb landing
4,570 lb takeoff; 4,342 lb landing
why: The AFM and the weight placard give 4,200 lb maximum takeoff and 4,000 lb maximum landing weight.

q: What is the Seneca I aft CG limit?

d: 87.9 in aft of datum at all weights
94.6 in at 4,200 lb, less when lighter
96.6 in aft of datum at all weights

q: What is the forward CG limit at the 4,200 lb maximum weight?
a: 87.9 in aft of datum
d: 80.7 in aft of datum
82.0 in aft of datum
94.6 in aft of datum
why: The forward limit is 80.7 in at 2,780 lb, 82.0 in at 3,400 lb and 87.9 in at 4,200 lb, varying in a straight line between points.

87.9 in aft of datum
About 83.5 in aft of datum

q: Where is the Seneca I datum?

78.4 in forward of the firewall face, on the fuselage centerline
78.4 in aft of the propeller spinner tip, along the thrust line

q: What is the Seneca I usable fuel capacity?

46.5 gal total in four tanks
45 gal per side, 90 gal total
why: Usable fuel is 46.5 gallons per side (two interconnected tanks each), 93 gallons total; the filler placard reads 'usable capacity 46.5 gal.' Unusable fuel is 2.5 gallons per side, so 98 gallons is the total including unusable.

q: What are the Seneca I baggage compartment limits?
a: 100 lb forward and 100 lb aft

200 lb forward and 100 lb aft
150 lb forward and 150 lb aft

q: What flap settings does the AFM give for normal takeoff and landing?
a: Takeoff 0°; landing 40°
d: Takeoff 10°; landing 40°
Takeoff 25°; landing 25°
Takeoff 0°; landing 25°
why: Section II lists takeoff 0° and landing 40°. 25° is the AFM's recommendation for a single-engine landing, not a normal one.

q: How are the Seneca I flaps operated, and what does each handle notch give?

d: Electrically; 10°, 25° and 40°
Manually; 15°, 25° and 40°
Hydraulically; 10°, 20° and 40°
why: The flaps are manually operated: first notch 10°, second 25°, third 40°.

a: Flaps retract to 25°
d: Landing gear up
Flaps fully retracted
Cowl flaps closed
why: School go-around: throttles full forward, pitch up 10–12°, flaps to 25°, landing gear up once the VSI shows a positive rate of climb, the remaining flaps below 125 MPH, then adjust the cowl flaps. (The printed AFM, POH 3-7, lists positive climb, flaps, then gear.)

q: What does the AFM preflight check of the alternator system confirm?

OV lights stay out with both alternator switches off
Battery voltage rises as each alternator switch cycles
why: The check confirms the overvoltage lights operate and both ammeters show roughly equal outputs with both engines at 1500 RPM or more. Both alternator switches stay ON for normal operation.

q: Except during engine cranking, what is the maximum output for each alternator?

d: 50 amperes
70 amperes
40 amperes
why: Normal output should not exceed 60 A per alternator except while cranking. The emergency procedures limit the load to 50 A when relying on one alternator.

q: What must you do to use the press-to-test feature of an overvoltage trip light?
a: Turn that alternator switch OFF
d: Turn the master switch OFF
Pull that alternator's circuit breaker
Reduce that engine to idle RPM
why: The AFM says the alternator switch must be OFF to use the press-to-test feature. The school run-up does this one alternator at a time.

q: What is the normal fuel system setup for takeoff and landing?
a: Selectors ON; electric fuel pumps ON
d: Selectors ON; electric fuel pumps OFF
Selectors X-FEED; electric fuel pumps ON
Selectors ON; one electric pump ON
why: For takeoff and landing both selectors are ON and both electric pumps ON. In cruise the selectors stay ON and the pumps go OFF.

q: Per the AFM, what can a fast taxi turn just before the takeoff run cause if the electric boost pumps are not ON?
a: Temporary malfunction of one engine during takeoff
d: Vapor lock in both engines during the climb
Overheating of the electric fuel pump motors
Fuel venting overboard through the tank vents
why: The AFM 'Turning takeoffs' note warns that fast taxi turns right before the takeoff run can briefly upset one engine's fuel supply on takeoff unless the boost pumps are ON. That is one reason the pumps are ON for takeoff and landing.

q: How are the Seneca I fuel tanks treated for tank selection?
a: Each side's two interconnected tanks count as one
d: Each of the four tanks is selected separately
Inboard tanks feed first, then outboard tanks
All four tanks feed one common manifold
why: Each engine normally draws from the two interconnected tanks on its own side, and the AFM treats them as a single tank for selection.

q: With both engines running in cruise, may both engines be fed from the same tank?
a: Yes, it is permissible in cruising flight
d: No, crossfeed is for single-engine use only
Yes, but only for takeoff and landing
Only with both electric pumps ON
why: The AFM says it is permissible to operate both engines from the same tank in cruising flight. Crossfeed is used in level flight only.

q: When does the gear warning horn sound, per the AFM?
a: At low throttle settings with the gear up
d: Below 125 MPH with the gear up
When flaps pass 25° with the gear up
Whenever airspeed is below 105 MPH
why: The horn sounds at low throttle settings with the gear up. On serial numbers 34-7250046 and up, which includes your Seneca (s/n 34-7350315), the red gear light also comes on whenever the horn sounds.

q: What maximum altitude loss does the AFM give for a power-off stall?

Up to 250 ft in either configuration
Up to 500 ft clean; 300 ft with gear and flaps down
why: The AFM says a power-off stall may lose up to 450 ft with gear and flaps up and also up to 450 ft with gear down and 40° flaps.

q: What maximum altitude loss does the AFM give for a power-on stall, clean versus gear down and 40° flaps?

Up to 400 ft clean; up to 550 ft with gear and flaps down
Up to 550 ft in either configuration
why: Power-on stalls may lose up to 550 ft with gear and flaps up and up to 400 ft with gear down and 40° flaps.

q: When is the Seneca I stall warning system inoperative?
a: With the master switch off
d: With the flaps beyond 25°
With the pitot heat off
With the gear down and locked
why: The stall warning is electric, and the AFM states it is inoperative with the master switch off.

q: For flight into known icing, what propeller ice protection must be installed?

Pneumatic propeller boots
Heated spinners only

q: An airplane has only the windshield heating installation, not the full ice package. What does the placard left of the engine controls say?

Compass unreliable with windshield heat on

Windshield heat, wing deice and pitot heat

After 1 inch of ice accumulates
Continuously, every 60 seconds in icing

Turn off pitot heat to reduce the load

The surface deice switch
The master switch, automatically

Up to 25 MPH
Up to 20 MPH

Set 2700 RPM and hold altitude
Extend 10° flaps to lower the stall speed

They share one fuel supply line

q: With coordinated controls, how does the AFM say you detect a dead engine?

RPM drop; nose pitches down sharply
Loss of thrust; roll away from the dead engine
why: The AFM lists two cues: loss of thrust, and the nose yawing toward the dead engine. The good engine's thrust swings the nose toward the failed side.

q: Per your school's engine-failure memory items, the first step is 'maintain direction and airspeed' at what speed?
a: 105 MPH (blue line)
d: 80 MPH (red line)
120 MPH (en route climb)
76 MPH (bottom of green arc)
why: School memory items: maintain direction and airspeed, blue line 105 MPH (Vyse); then mixtures, props and throttles forward, flaps up, gear up, fuel pumps on, identify and verify. (The printed AFM, POH 3-11, says to maintain airspeed above 90 MPH.)

q: Per the AFM feathering procedure, after mixtures, props and throttles forward, what are the next three steps?
a: Flaps retract, gear retract, electric fuel pumps ON
d: Identify, verify, then feather the inoperative engine
Gear retract, flaps retract, cowl flaps open on both
Electric fuel pumps ON, identify, then gear retract
why: The AFM order is mixtures, props, throttles forward; flaps up; gear up; electric pumps ON; then identify, retard the throttle to verify, and feather.

q: Why does the AFM have you retard the throttle of the suspected inoperative engine before feathering?
a: To verify it is the failed engine before feathering
d: To cut drag from the windmilling prop before feathering
To keep the failed engine from overspeeding its prop
To slow the prop below 800 RPM so it can feather
why: 'Throttle of inoperative engine - retard to verify.' Feathering the wrong (good) engine would leave you with no power, so confirm first.

q: You retard the throttle of the engine you think failed, and yaw and power noticeably change. What does that tell you?
a: Wrong engine; re-advance it and re-identify
d: Engine verified dead; feather it
Governor failed; pull the prop to low RPM
Engine flooded; pull its mixture to cutoff
why: Pulling back the dead engine's throttle changes nothing. A change in yaw or power means that engine was producing thrust, so restore it and identify again before feathering.

q: Immediately after feathering the propeller, what is the next AFM step?
a: Mixture of the inoperative engine to idle cutoff
d: Magnetos of the inoperative engine OFF
Fuel selector of the inoperative engine OFF
Electric fuel pump of the inoperative engine OFF
why: After 'Propeller - feather' comes 'Mixture - idle cut off,' then trim, 5° bank, inoperative-engine pump OFF, magnetos OFF, cowl flaps, alternator OFF, electrical load, fuel OFF.

q: After feathering, how much bank does the AFM say to hold, and which way?
a: 5° toward the operating engine
d: 5° toward the inoperative engine
10° toward the operating engine
Wings level with the ball centered
why: Banking toward the good engine lets the horizontal component of lift help the rudder counter the yaw, reducing sideslip and drag.

q: If circumstances permit, the AFM suggests trying to restore power before feathering. Which set matches its suggestions?
a: Mixture as required, boost pump on, crossfeed, L or R mag, alt air on
d: Mixture lean, boost pump off, selector off, both mags, alt air off
Mixture rich, boost pump off, selector on, both mags, carb heat on
Mixture cutoff, boost pump on, crossfeed, mags off, alt air on
why: The AFM note lists: mixture as required, fuel boost pump on, fuel selector crossfeed, magnetos L or R only, alternate air on.

q: Why does the AFM direct feathering the propeller of a failed engine?
a: Single-engine performance decreases if it is not feathered
d: A windmilling prop will overspeed the propeller governor
Feathering is required before any in-flight restart
It keeps the stop pins from engaging as the engine slows
why: A windmilling prop creates large drag. The AFM states single-engine performance will decrease if the inoperative prop is not feathered.

q: Per your school's air-start checklist, what is the first step to unfeather and restart an engine?
a: Fuel selector of the inoperative engine ON
d: Starter engaged until the prop windmills
Mixture of the inoperative engine rich
Propeller control full forward
why: School air start: fuel selector (inop engine) ON, its fuel pump OFF, throttle open 1/4 inch, prop control full forward, mixture rich, magnetos ON, starter until the prop windmills, throttle reduced until the engine is warm, zero thrust set, alternator ON, cowl flaps open when warm.

q: In the Seneca I AFM unfeathering procedure, what gets the feathered propeller turning?
a: Engaging the starter until the prop windmills
d: An unfeathering accumulator, as the prop moves forward
Diving until the prop windmills above 800 RPM
Turning the electric fuel pump on for 3 seconds
why: The AFM procedure uses the starter: 'Starter - engage till prop windmills.' It has no accumulator step.

q: Per your school's air-start checklist, where does the propeller control go when unfeathering?
a: Full forward (high RPM)
d: In the feather detent until the engine fires
Full aft (low RPM) until the engine is warm
Left where it was before the engine failed
why: The school air-start checklist sets the propeller control full forward, then engages the starter until the prop windmills. (The printed AFM, POH 3-12, says forward to the cruise RPM position.)

q: Single-engine cruise: you want fuel from the tank on the dead engine's side. How are the selectors set?
a: Operating engine X-FEED; inoperative engine OFF
d: Operating engine ON; inoperative engine X-FEED
Both selectors X-FEED
Operating engine X-FEED; inoperative engine ON
why: The operating engine's selector goes to X-FEED and the dead engine's to OFF; electric pumps stay OFF unless the operating engine's driven pump fails. Crossfeed exists to increase single-engine range and is used in level flight only.

q: For a single-engine landing, how does the AFM set up the fuel system?
a: Operating ON, inop OFF, operating electric pump ON
d: Operating X-FEED, inop OFF, both electric pumps OFF
Both selectors ON, both electric pumps ON for landing
Operating ON, inop OFF, all electric pumps OFF
why: For landing: operating engine selector ON, inoperative engine OFF, and the operating engine's electric pump ON.

q: An engine fails during the takeoff roll at 85 MPH CAS. What does the AFM say to do?
a: Close both throttles immediately; stop straight ahead
d: Continue the takeoff and feather once safely airborne
Close only the failed engine's throttle and stop
Rotate early at 90 MPH and climb out at 105 MPH
why: If the failure happens on the ground roll before 100 MPH CAS, the AFM says close both throttles immediately and stop straight ahead.

q: After an abort below 100 MPH, the remaining runway is inadequate to stop. What does the AFM add?
a: Max braking, master OFF, fuel selectors OFF
d: Gear up, feather both props, flaps up
Max braking, mixtures rich, props forward
Flaps up, master ON, electric pumps ON
why: With throttles closed: apply maximum braking, master switch OFF, fuel selectors OFF, and continue straight ahead, turning to avoid obstacles as needed.

q: An engine fails just after liftoff, gear still down, at 102 MPH CAS, with plenty of runway left. What does the AFM say?
a: Close both throttles, land, and stop straight ahead
d: Retract the gear and continue the climb at 105 MPH
Feather the dead engine and climb straight ahead
Lower the nose to 105 MPH and circle back to land
why: At or above 100 MPH with gear down, if adequate runway remains: close both throttles immediately, land if airborne, and stop straight ahead.

q: You decide to continue after an engine failure on takeoff. What order does the AFM give?
a: Hold heading and airspeed, gear up once climbing, feather
d: Feather, then gear up, then hold heading and airspeed
Gear up immediately, feather, then establish the climb
Hold heading, feather, then raise the gear at 500 ft AGL
why: If continuing: maintain heading and airspeed, retract the gear when a climb is established, then feather. The AFM bases the continue/abort decision on loading, density altitude, obstructions, weather and pilot competence.

q: An engine fails in the climb at 78 MPH CAS. What does the AFM say to do first?
a: Reduce power on the good engine to keep directional control
d: Full power on both engines and feather the dead engine
Raise the nose to hold altitude, then feather the dead engine
Feather the dead engine first, then lower the nose
why: Below the 80 MPH Vmc, full power on the good engine can yaw the airplane beyond rudder authority. Reduce that power as needed to keep directional control.

q: Below Vmc after an engine failure, you have reduced power on the good engine. What does the AFM say next?
a: Lower the nose toward 105 MPH, then feather
d: Feather first, then lower the nose to hold 90 MPH
Hold the attitude, add rudder trim, then feather
Lower the nose to 80 MPH and hold it there
why: The AFM: reduce nose attitude to accelerate toward the 105 MPH single-engine best rate-of-climb speed, then feather the inoperative engine.

q: An engine fails in the climb at 95 MPH CAS. What are the AFM steps?
a: Maintain control, adjust toward 105 MPH, feather
d: Reduce good-engine power, lower nose, feather
Maintain control, slow to 90 MPH, feather
Feather, then accelerate to 120 MPH
why: Above 80 MPH: maintain directional control, adjust airspeed toward 105 MPH (Vyse), and feather the inoperative engine.

q: Per the AFM (POH 3-13), when should the landing gear and wing flaps be extended for a single-engine landing?
a: Not until certain of making the field
d: At the final approach fix, as usual
Gear on downwind, flaps on base
Gear at 1,000 ft AGL, flaps at 500 ft AGL
why: The AFM says do not extend the landing gear or lower the flaps until certain of making the field. Their drag on one engine can make a go-around impossible.

q: What final approach speed and flap setting does the AFM recommend for a single-engine landing?
a: 105 MPH with 25° flaps
d: 90 MPH with 40° flaps
105 MPH with 40° flaps
87 MPH with 25° flaps
why: A final approach at 105 MPH using 25° rather than full flaps puts the airplane in the best configuration for a go-around, should one be needed.

q: Why does the AFM recommend 25° rather than full flaps for a single-engine landing?
a: It leaves the airplane best set up for a go-around
d: 40° flaps exceed the single-engine flap speed limit
Full flaps blank the rudder at low airspeeds
The stall speed is lower with 25° than with 40°
why: Less flap means less drag if power must be added. Even so, the AFM says a single-engine go-around should be avoided if at all possible and may be impossible under some loading and density altitude conditions.

q: Per the AFM single-engine go-around, after mixture, prop and throttle forward, what comes next?
a: Flaps retract, then landing gear retract
d: Landing gear retract, then flaps retract
Cowl flaps open, then landing gear retract
Trim set, then flaps retract to 25°
why: AFM sequence: mixture, prop, throttle forward; flaps up; gear up; airspeed 105 MPH (Vyse); trim set; cowl flap as required on the operating engine.

q: Before a daytime manual gear extension, the AFM has you turn the navigation lights OFF. Why?
a: Gear lights dim with nav lights on, hard to see by day
d: The nav lights share a circuit with the hydraulic gear pump
It frees electrical power for the emergency gear extension
The gear warning horn is disabled with the nav lights on
why: The AFM notes the gear indicator lights are dimmed while the navigation lights are on, so in daylight you might not see three greens. The other pre-checks are circuit breakers, master ON and alternators.

q: What is the maximum airspeed for manual (emergency) gear extension?
a: 100 MPH
d: 125 MPH
150 MPH
105 MPH
why: The AFM says reduce power with airspeed not to exceed 100 MPH, then put the selector DOWN, pull the emergency knob and check three greens.

q: After an emergency gear extension due to a malfunction, how long should the knob stay pulled out?
a: Until the airplane is on jacks and the gear systems are checked
d: Until the landing rollout is complete and the airplane is parked
Until the red unsafe light goes out after touchdown
Until the next 100-hour inspection is completed
why: The AFM warning says leave the control out until the airplane is on jacks to check the gear's hydraulic and electrical systems. The placard says 'See A.F.M. before re-engagement.'

q: When does the red landing gear unsafe light illuminate on your Seneca (s/n 34-7350315)?
a: Gear in transit, or whenever the gear horn sounds
d: Only when the gear is up and locked
Only when a gear leg fails to lock down
Gear in transit, or whenever the stall horn sounds
why: The light shows the gear in transition. On serial numbers 34-7250046 and up, which includes 34-7350315, it also lights whenever the gear warning horn sounds. It is off when the gear is fully up, or down and locked.

q: After a normal gear extension the red unsafe light stays on. What does the AFM say to do?
a: Recycle the landing gear
d: Pull the emergency gear knob immediately
Land; it is only an indication fault
Pull the gear pump circuit breaker
why: The red light means the gear is between fully up and down-and-locked. The AFM says to recycle the gear if the light stays on.

q: Why does the AFM say to leave the flaps up for a gear-up landing?
a: To reduce wing and flap damage
d: To lower the touchdown speed
To keep the stall warning working
To keep the CG within limits
why: Gear-up landing: approach with power at normal speed, flaps up to limit damage, close throttles just before touchdown, master and ignition OFF, fuel selectors OFF, touch down at minimum speed.

q: Per the AFM, both overvoltage lights come on. You turn off all loads except the master, and both alternator switches OFF. What next?
a: Turn each alternator on briefly, one at a time, watching ammeters
d: Turn both alternators on together and compare the two ammeters
Leave both alternators off and land on battery power alone
Cycle the master switch off, then back on after 10 seconds
why: The AFM has you briefly switch each alternator ON, one at a time, to compare outputs, then keep the one showing the least output.

q: Per the AFM both-overvoltage-lights procedure, which alternator do you turn back ON?
a: The one showing the LEAST output
d: The one showing the MOST output
Either one; they are identical
The one on the critical engine
why: A failed regulator drives its alternator's output up uncontrollably, so the lower-output alternator is the healthy one. Then keep the load at or below 50 A.

q: After an overvoltage trip or loss of one alternator, what electrical load limit does the AFM give?
a: Do not exceed 50 amperes
d: Do not exceed 60 amperes
Do not exceed 30 amperes
Do not exceed 70 amperes
why: The electrical failure procedures repeatedly limit output to 50 A. 60 A is the normal maximum per alternator.

q: Per your school checklist, one overvoltage light comes on. After loads off and that alternator OFF, what next?
a: Alternator ON; if more than 50 amps, OFF; load 50 A max
d: Reset its circuit breaker, then leave it ON at any load
Turn the other alternator OFF and keep this one ON
Leave it OFF and the master OFF for the rest of the flight
why: School checklist (Overvoltage Light — One): all electrical load off, master on, that alternator off, then on — if it shows more than 50 amps, off — and keep electrical equipment to no more than 50 amps. (The printed AFM, POH 3-15, switches it on only momentarily to confirm excessive output, then leaves it off.)

q: One alternator loses output (no overvoltage light). What does the AFM say to do?
a: Load 50 A max, check breakers, cycle that alternator OFF then ON
d: Load 60 A max, check breakers, cycle the master OFF then ON
Turn off the good alternator, then reset both overvoltage relays
Shed all electrical loads and land immediately
why: If cycling the switch does not restore output, keep the load at or below 50 A to continue, and get maintenance before further flight.

q: What warning does the AFM give when both alternators are inoperative?
a: Compass error may exceed 10°
d: Fuel gauges will read inaccurately
Vacuum instruments will be unreliable
Gear position lights will not work
why: The AFM warns that compass error may exceed 10° with both alternators inoperative.

q: What does the red button annunciator in the vacuum system indicate?
a: A feathered engine or failed vacuum pump
d: Vacuum above the 5.2 in. Hg upper limit
A clogged gyro instrument air filter
Low oil pressure to that engine's prop governor
why: Each engine drives a vacuum pump. The red button shows when one pump is not supplying vacuum, whether because it failed or its engine is feathered.

q: Vacuum reads below 4.5 in. Hg. What does the AFM say to do?
a: Increase RPM to 2700; descend if needed to hold 4.5
d: Reduce RPM to 2200 and climb to cooler, denser air
Shut down the engine with the failed vacuum pump
Turn on the standby electric vacuum pump and continue
why: Raise RPM to 2700, descend if possible to where 4.5 in. Hg can be held, and use the electric turn indicator to monitor the attitude and heading indicators.

q: Engine fire in flight. What is the first AFM step for the affected engine?
a: Fuel selector OFF
d: Throttle CLOSE
Mixture IDLE CUT OFF
Propeller FEATHER
why: AFM order for the affected engine: fuel selector OFF, throttle close, propeller feather, mixture idle cutoff; then heater OFF and defroster OFF (in all cases of fire), and land immediately if terrain permits.

q: Engine fire in flight: after fuel selector OFF and throttle closed, what comes next?
a: Propeller FEATHER, then mixture IDLE CUT OFF
d: Mixture IDLE CUT OFF, then propeller FEATHER
Magnetos OFF, then cowl flaps OPEN
Propeller FEATHER, then master switch OFF
why: The AFM feathers the prop before the mixture goes to idle cutoff, then turns off the heater and defroster and lands immediately if terrain permits.

q: An engine catches fire during start, before it is running. What does the AFM say to do?
a: Mixture idle cutoff, throttle open, keep cranking
d: Stop cranking, fuel selector OFF, evacuate
Mixture rich, throttle closed, keep cranking
Master OFF, magnetos OFF, evacuate
why: Cranking with the mixture at idle cutoff and the throttle open tries to pull the fire into the engine. If it persists more than a few seconds, use external extinguishing with fuel selectors OFF.

q: A fire starts during engine start, but the engine has started and is running. What does the AFM say?
a: Keep it running to pull the fire into the engine
d: Shut it down at once with the mixture cutoff
Reduce to idle and turn the electric fuel pump off
Shut it down, then restart it to clear the fire
why: Keep the engine running to try to draw the fire in. If the fire lasts more than a few seconds, put it out by the best available external means, with fuel selectors OFF and mixture at idle cutoff.

q: In an unintentional spin, what is the AFM's first recovery step?
a: Retard both throttles to idle
d: Full rudder opposite the rotation
Control wheel full forward
Ailerons opposite the rotation
why: AFM order: throttles idle, full opposite rudder, release back pressure (push full forward if the nose doesn't drop), ailerons neutral, hold until rotation stops, neutralize rudder, smooth pull-out.

q: Why does the AFM warn against abrupt control movement in the dive after spin recovery?
a: The positive limit load factor may be exceeded
d: It can overspeed both propellers in the dive
It can unport the fuel pickups in the tanks
It can restart the rotation in the opposite direction
why: Pull out of the dive with smooth back pressure; an abrupt pull can exceed the 3.8 G positive limit maneuvering load factor.

q: An engine fails in icing conditions. What does the AFM say to try first?
a: Select alternate air and attempt a restart
d: Feather immediately and descend out of the ice
Close the cowl flaps to warm it, then attempt a restart
Increase RPM to 2700 to shed ice from the prop
why: Induction icing may be the cause, so select ALTERNATE AIR and try to restart. If it won't restart, feather and follow the icing engine-out steps.

q: The engine won't restart after a failure in icing. What minimum airspeed does the AFM specify?
a: 105 MPH CAS, including on final
d: 90 MPH CAS, then 80 MPH on final
105 MPH CAS, then 90 MPH on final
120 MPH CAS, then 105 MPH on final
why: Maintain at least 105 MPH CAS, descending if needed to hold it; reduce electrical loads, avoid further icing, land as soon as practical, keep 105 MPH on final, and use 25° rather than full flaps. Gear and flaps wait until certain of making the field.

q: An alternator fails in icing and can't be restored. Which avionics does the AFM say to keep on?
a: One NAV/COM and the transponder
d: All avionics; shed windshield heat only
The autopilot and one NAV/COM
Only the transponder
why: Also turn off the electric windshield to hold a 60 A load and leave icing as soon as practical. The windshield may be turned on before landing; the battery may run down and the gear may need free-fall extension.
drop_reason: N56307 not equipped: procedure is built around the electric windshield

q: What is the first step if a propeller overspeeds?
a: Close the throttle
d: Pull the prop control to feather
Pull the mixture to idle cutoff
Raise the nose to slow to Vx
why: Overspeed procedure: close throttle, slow to best rate-of-climb speed, prop control back to low RPM, slowly add throttle until the governor engages, then set power. Continue at reduced speed and power and land as soon as practical.

q: Propeller overspeed: after closing the throttle and slowing to best rate-of-climb speed, what is next?
a: Pull the prop control back to low RPM
d: Move the prop control to feather
Advance the throttle to re-engage the governor
Shut down the engine with mixture cutoff
why: With the prop control at low RPM, slowly increase throttle until the governor takes hold, then slowly bring prop and throttle up to the desired setting.

q: The cabin combustion heater overheats. What happens, per the AFM?
a: Fuel, air and ignition to the heater cut off automatically
d: The heater fan speeds up to cool the combustion chamber
The heater keeps running at low output until it is reset
Only the ignition cuts off; fuel continues to flow
why: Overheat cuts off the heater automatically. Do not restart it until it has been inspected and the cause found and corrected. The overheat light on the heater console comes on as well.

q: With the AltiMatic IIIB-1 engaged, an engine fails. What does the supplement say to do?
a: Disengage, retrim ball centered, do engine-out procedure, re-engage
d: Leave it engaged and let it hold heading while you secure the engine
Select heading hold, then perform the normal engine-out procedure
Disengage and do not re-engage it at any time before landing
why: The supplement says disengage and retrim, keep the airplane in trim with the ball centered throughout, perform the normal engine-out procedure, then re-engage.
drop_reason: autopilot model unknown: AltiMatic IIIB-1 single-engine procedure; not common to all supplements

q: Per the FAA-approved AFM limitations, what is the maximum speed for extending even the first notch (10°) of flaps?
a: 125 MPH, the single Vfe for every setting
d: 160 MPH, from the staged flap table
140 MPH, the second-notch figure
150 MPH, the gear-extended limit
why: The AFM limitations give one maximum flaps-extended speed, 125 MPH CAS, which is also the top of the white arc and the placarded figure. POH 6-10 prints higher staged speeds for 10° and 25°, but that is not the approved limitation; POH 7-1 also says flaps may be lowered up to 125 MPH.

q: What is the placarded maximum speed for opening the storm window?
a: 150 MPH
d: 125 MPH
133 MPH
105 MPH
why: The storm window placard reads 'Do not open above 150 MPH.' 150 MPH is also the gear-extended limit and the doors-removed maximum speed.

q: Per the instrument panel placard, when must the oil cooler winterization plate be removed?
a: When ambient temperature exceeds 50°F
d: When ambient temperature exceeds 32°F
When oil temperature exceeds 245°F
When ambient temperature exceeds 70°F
why: The placard says to remove the winterization plate when the ambient temperature exceeds 50°F. Left on in warm weather, it restricts oil cooling.

q: Where are the Seneca I circuit breakers, and how does the AFM say to reset one?
a: Lower right of the panel; push in the reset button
d: Lower left of the panel; pull out, then push in
Overhead panel; toggle the breaker off, then on
Lower right of the panel; cycle the master switch
why: All circuit breakers are grouped in the lower right corner of the instrument panel and are reset by pushing in the button. The Operating Tips (POH 7-1) add a two to five minute cooling period before resetting.

q: Single-engine cruise with the electric pumps OFF: when does the AFM say the operating engine's electric fuel pump must be used?
a: If its engine-driven fuel pump fails
d: Whenever crossfeed is selected
Whenever the dead engine is feathered
Whenever above 10,000 ft density altitude
why: In single-engine cruise the electric pumps stay OFF, from the same side or on crossfeed, except that an engine-driven pump failure requires the electric pump on the operating engine's side. It goes back ON for the landing.

q: Per the AFM, how does removing the rear cabin and cargo doors affect climb and cruise performance?
a: Both are reduced by about 5 percent
d: Both are reduced by about 15 percent
Climb drops 5 percent; cruise is unchanged
No change; only Vmc rises to 81 MPH
why: All climb and cruise performance drops about five percent with the doors off. The doors-off limits also include 150 MPH maximum, 81 MPH Vmc and VFR non-icing only.

q: If the electric pitch trim malfunctions, how does its AFM supplement say to disengage it?
a: Operate the push-button trim switch on the instrument panel
d: Depress the center bar on the control wheel switch
Pull the stabilator trim cable release knob
Cycle both alternator switches OFF, then ON
why: The supplement says to disengage electric trim with the push-button trim switch on the panel, and in an emergency it can be overpowered with the manual trim wheel. Pressing the center bar is part of normal operation, not a disconnect.
